question.text: Metastatic carcinoma to the cervical nodes from an unknown head and neck primary site: Is there a need for neck dissection?
question.context: The aim of the study was to evaluate the outcomes and patterns of failure in patients with metastatic carcinoma to cervical lymph nodes from an unknown head and neck primary origin, who were treated curatively with radiotherapy, with or without neck dissection. The study included 61 patients referred to the McGill University Hospital Centers from 1987 to 2002. The median age was 57 years, with male to female ratio of 4:1. Distribution of patients by N status was as follows: N1, 16 patients (26%); N2a, 18 (30%); N2b, 13 (22%); N2c, 7 (11%); and N3, 7 (11%). Twenty patients underwent neck dissection (11 radical, 9 functional) and 41 patients had biopsy (9 fine-needle aspiration and 32 excisional biopsy). All patients received radiotherapy. The median dose to the involved node(s) was 64 Gy, and 60 Gy to the rest of the neck. Treatment of the neck was bilateral in 50 patients (82%) and ipsilateral in 11 (18%). The minimum duration of the follow-up was 12 months, with the median of 32 months. The 5- and 8-year overall survival for the whole population was 79% and 67%, respectively. There was no statistically significant difference in the 8-year actuarial overall survival (64.8% and 67.6%, respectively, p = .64) and local relapse-free survival (75% vs 74.5%, respectively, p = .57), among patients who had biopsy versus those who had neck dissection.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study evaluated outcomes in patients with metastatic cervical node disease from an unknown head and neck primary. The study found no statistically significant difference in overall survival or local relapse-free survival between patients who underwent neck dissection and those who did not. This suggests that neck dissection is not necessarily required for improved outcomes in this specific patient population.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: There was no statistically significant difference in the 8-year actuarial overall survival (64.8% and 67.6%, respectively, p = .64) and local relapse-free survival (75% vs 74.5%, respectively, p = .57), among patients who had biopsy versus those who had neck dissection.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study doesn't explicitly address the role of neck dissection in all head and neck cancers, the lack of a survival benefit in this specific group of patients with unknown primary suggests that it may not be necessary. Other factors, such as patient comorbidities and tumor characteristics, could influence the decision to perform a neck dissection.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study shows no significant difference in survival between patients who underwent neck dissection and those who had biopsy or no surgery. With a median survival of 79% at 5 years and no statistically significant difference in outcomes, the evidence suggests that neck dissection may not be necessary for these patients.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: No statistically significant difference in 8-year actuarial overall survival (64.8% vs 67.6%) and local relapse-free survival (75% vs 74.5%) between biopsy and neck dissection groups
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered whether unknown primary site might affect treatment approach, but the study specifically focused on this population and found no significant benefit from neck dissection. Also considered if higher N stage would change recommendation, but even N3 patients showed similar outcomes to those with lower N stages.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study showed no statistically significant difference in overall survival or local relapse-free survival between patients who underwent neck dissection versus those who had biopsy, indicating that neck dissection does not confer a survival advantage in this population. Given the lack of benefit and the potential morbidity of surgery, neck dissection is not indicated.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: There was no statistically significant difference in 8-year overall survival (64.8% vs 67.6%, p = .64) or local relapse-free survival (75% vs 74.5%, p = .57) between patients who had biopsy versus those who had neck dissection.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Differential diagnoses such as primary tumors in the oral cavity, oropharynx, or larynx were considered, but the case specifies an unknown primary, making neck dissection unnecessary without evidence of benefit from the study.

olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: The case describes metastatic carcinoma to cervical nodes from an unknown primary in the head and neck, with no statistically significant difference in overall or relapse-free survival between patients who had neck dissection and those who did not. This suggests that neck dissection does not improve outcomes in this context, where the primary site remains undetermined. Since the benefit of neck dissection is most supported in cases with a confirmed primary, the answer is not clearly 'yes'. However, 'no' would be incorrect because some patients did receive neck dissection. 'maybe' is the most cautious and evidence-based choice, acknowledging uncertainty but noting the lack of survival benefit from dissection in this unproven primary scenario.
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: The absence of a statistically significant difference in 5-year and 8-year overall survival and local relapse-free survival between biopsy-only and dissection-included groups.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Cervical metastases from unknown primary vs. confirmed primary site; the latter typically justifies neck dissection. However, since the primary is unknown and dissection did not confer a survival benefit in this unselected group, recommending dissection is not justified.
